deep.reconstruction:
The page has no handwritten text. It is a sheet of 1983-84 Montpellier computer listing paper; the reversed show-through reads 'DATASETS PICTURES … SYSMSG … CNU M06 …'. Grothendieck covered it with six coloured-felt-pen sketches belonging to his study of systems of pseudo-lines (topological arrangements of curves in the real projective plane, each behaving like a line). Read in that context, the figures seem to be local and global pictures of the cell decomposition such an arrangement induces.

(1) Top centre: a vertex (orange dot) joined by solid and dashed edges to the vertices of a pentagon-like polygon (green and blue sides, partly dashed). This looks like the cone or star of a vertex over the boundary of a 2-cell, i.e. a barycentric-type subdivision or 'umbrella' of a polygonal face. Solid versus dashed may mark visible versus hidden edges, or two kinds of edges in a dual decomposition.

(2) Left centre: a 'flower' with about 8-10 petals around a point, crossed by blue lines through that point. This plausibly shows the neighbourhood of a multiple point (several pseudo-lines through one point). The petals stand for the sectors or small regions near the point, or for blowing up the point so the lines become separated directions on a circle.

(3) Right centre: a regular-looking network of green segments meeting at nodes in a roughly triangular/hexagonal pattern (a piece of a simple arrangement or its dual graph). Superimposed are the same flower and a fan of blue and dark-red curves out of it. One blue/red curve is drawn doubled with hatching, perhaps a distinguished pseudo-line or a boundary. This suggests comparing a multiple point with a nearby simple arrangement (a perturbation or 'resolution' of the multiple point), or drawing the dual cell structure on top of the primal one.

(4) Bottom left: an orange circle with three blue lines and three paler lines through its centre, over a faint pencil sketch of a larger polygon. This is probably a small disc around a crossing point, where 2k half-lines cut the boundary circle. It may also be the model of the projective plane as a disc with antipodal boundary identification.

(5) Bottom centre: a square with a green 'tic-tac-toe' cross. This looks like a local grid model of two families of pseudo-lines, or a quadrilateral cell subdivided.

(6) Bottom right: a curved (Reuleaux-like / spherical) triangle with three green lines from an interior vertex. A hatched black arc and a lens-shaped shaded region are attached. This plausibly shows a triangular cell of an arrangement (simple arrangements always have triangles, by Levi's and Roudneff's results) with an adjoining region, or a crosscap/Möbius-band neighbourhood of a line drawn on the projective plane.

Overall the sheet seems to explore local combinatorics (stars of vertices, multiple points, triangles) and the passage between an arrangement and a dual decomposition. Nothing on it is a precise statement.
errors: No mathematical claims are written, so nothing can be checked. The interpretations above are conjectural readings of unlabeled drawings.

The figures plausibly depict standard local configurations of pseudo-line arrangements and cell decompositions, so nothing identifiable goes beyond the known literature. Its interest is documentary: it shows Grothendieck's visual working method in the pseudo-line notes.
